theme: The Entry; the Temple; controversies; the widow’s offering
readingInstruction: Read Mark 11:1-12:44. The Entry into Jerusalem, the cursing of the fig tree, the cleansing of the temple, and a series of controversies in the temple courts, ending with the widow’s offering. Notice how Jesus answers each question and then asks his own.
settingTheScene: Mark has taken ten chapters to bring Jesus to Jerusalem, and now he slows down: more than a third of the Gospel is devoted to this last week. Jesus rides in on a colt, goes into the temple, and curses a fig tree, using it as a sign of judgment on a barren temple. Then he teaches in the temple courts, where various groups try to trap him.
observation: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” (11:9).
“Is it not written, My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations? But you have made it a den of robbers” (11:17).
“And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses” (11:25).
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (12:10).
“And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength” (12:30).
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (12:31).
“Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box” (12:43).
interpretation:
Jesus sends two disciples for a colt, and he enters Jerusalem to the shouts of the crowd. Mark’s entry is quiet compared to the others. Jesus enters the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves, since it is already late. The next morning he curses a barren fig tree, and then he cleanses the temple, driving out the buyers and sellers. The fig tree is wrapped around the temple scene: Mark places the cursing before and the withering after, so that the barren tree interprets what happens in the temple. The temple was supposed to be a house of prayer for all nations. Instead, the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray, was filled with commerce. The leaders hear and seek to destroy him.

In the temple courts, they challenge his authority. He answers with a question about John’s baptism, and they cannot answer. Then he tells the parable of the tenants: the owner of a vineyard sends servants, and the tenants beat and kill them, and finally he sends his beloved son, and they kill him. It is clear to the leaders that he is speaking about them. Jesus quotes Psalm 118: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.”

The Pharisees and Herodians ask about paying taxes to Caesar, and the Sadducees ask about the resurrection. Jesus answers both: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob “is not God of the dead, but of the living.” A scribe asks which commandment is the most important. Jesus answers with the Shema and Leviticus 19: love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength, and love your neighbor as yourself. The scribe agrees, and Jesus says, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”

Then Jesus asks his own question: how can the Christ be David’s son, when David himself, in Psalm 110, says, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand”? The answer is that the Christ is both David’s son and David’s Lord. He warns against the scribes who devour widows’ houses and make long prayers for show. And then, in the last scene, he watches people give to the temple treasury. Many rich put in large sums. A poor widow puts in two small copper coins. Jesus calls the disciples: “This poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing… she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.” God sees the heart.
connection: Zechariah 9:9 is the colt. Psalm 118:25-26 is the hosanna. Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 are the temple verses. Isaiah 5:1-7 is the vineyard. Psalm 110:1 is the Lord at the right hand. Deuteronomy 6:4-5 and Leviticus 19:18 are the great commandments. Micah 7:1 and Hosea 9:10 use the fig tree as a picture of Israel. Exodus 3:6 is the God of Abraham. 2 Corinthians 8:1-5 praises generous giving in poverty.
application:
Ask what has crowded out prayer in your life, in your church. Clear a space.

Say the great commandment aloud: love God with your heart, soul, mind, and strength. Which part is hardest?

Give something sacrificial this week, however small, and know that God sees.
prayerPrompts: Welcome the King who comes in the name of the Lord.
Ask him to make his church a house of prayer for all nations.
Ask him to help you give your whole self.
